delusion

dih-LOO-zhun -- shares a root with 'illusion.' · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Delusion is a mistaken belief that is firmly held despite evidence that it is false.

His delusion that he would win the lottery without ever buying a ticket persisted for years.

Example

A man is absolutely convinced that his neighbors are secretly spying on him through the television, a delusion he holds onto even after friends and family repeatedly show him there is no evidence for it at all.

That firmly held false belief, kept alive despite clear evidence against it, is what makes it a delusion. Unlike 'assumption,' which can be reasonable, a delusion is specifically false and stubbornly maintained.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fantasy: A fantasy is a pleasant, imagined idea with little basis in reality -- a daydream you enjoy and can set aside at will. A delusion is no entertainment: it is a false belief someone genuinely holds and keeps defending even when the evidence says it is wrong.

illusion: An illusion is a false impression created by outside appearances -- a magician's trick, a heat shimmer on the road -- something that fools the senses. A delusion comes from inside: a mistaken belief a person's own mind builds and defends no matter what the outside evidence shows.

hallucination: A hallucination is a false perception produced by the mind itself -- seeing or hearing something with no outside source at all. A delusion is a false belief rather than a false sight or sound: the senses may work perfectly while the conviction itself stays wrong and firmly held.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

fact: something known to be true

reality: the state of things as they actually exist

Where it sits · how stubbornly the false idea is held — misconception → delusion → obsession

misconception vs. delusion: Misconception is milder than delusion -- a misconception can be a simple, correctable misunderstanding, while a delusion is a false belief held stubbornly, often despite clear proof otherwise.

obsession vs. delusion: An obsession holds on even harder than a delusion: a delusion is a false belief defended against all the evidence, while an obsession fills a person's thoughts so completely that the fixed idea leaves room for almost nothing else.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: down, thoroughly (Latin)

Root — lus

Root — lus: to play, trick, deceive (from Latin ludere, 'to play'; its stem lus- -- the same root spelled lud- in ludicrous)

Suffix — -ion

Suffix — -ion: the act, state, or result of (Latin -io)

Put it together

Put it together: De- ('thoroughly') + lus ('to play, trick', from Latin ludere) + -ion ('the state of') spell delusion. Latin deludere meant 'to deceive thoroughly' -- a delusion, at its root, is a thorough trick played on the mind and held onto as if it were true, the same root that gives us illusion.

Use the root in a new word: illusion

Use the root in a new word: illusion: The magician's illusion made the coin appear to vanish into thin air.

Word Choice

Delusion often appears in psychological or clinical contexts to describe a false belief maintained despite clear contrary evidence, though it is also used more loosely in everyday speech.
